summary: Design/experience paper from Bauplan Labs describing 'SDK 2.0' for their lakehouse: Python/SQL pipeline nodes carry Pydantic-style schema annotations (types, Required, enums, docs, lineage) that are enforced at three points (local type checker, control-plane DAG composition check against the catalog, worker runtime validation before persistence). Annotations are persisted to Iceberg metadata so agents can retrieve semantics via an MCP server for text-to-SQL. Illustrated on a three-node Titanic DAG; no quantitative evaluation.

claims.claim: Schema mismatches at node boundaries are a recurring, operationally important failure class across millions of production jobs
claims.evidence: §2.2 asserts this from operating experience with citations; no failure counts, rates, or job statistics from Bauplan are reported anywhere in the paper.

claims.claim: DAG-type contracts give each common failure (dropped column, nulls, type change, shifting semantics) a direct solution
claims.evidence: §4.1 walks through the four hand-constructed Titanic scenarios and states which enforcement step rejects them; illustration by construction, no measured catch rate or before/after comparison.

claims.claim: Persisting annotations in Iceberg metadata enables accurate agent SQL generation via MCP
claims.evidence: §4.2 and Fig. 3 describe the flow; no text-to-SQL accuracy experiment is reported.

claims.claim: Contracts compose across engines via Arrow types
claims.evidence: §4.4 design argument referencing connector docs; no cross-engine demonstration.

patterns.note: Typed data contracts at pipeline-node boundaries, checked pre-execution against catalog state; analogous to cross-repo interface contracts, but argued not measured.
Contract/schema declared in code before execution and enforced 'shift left'; spec-as-type, no evidence of effect on agents.
Local type checker plus control-plane static composition check as early feedback; no measurement.
MCP server exposing Iceberg metadata for agent text-to-SQL is described only.

methodology.sample: one illustrative three-node Titanic DAG; no dataset or task set
methodology.baselines: none; related work (dbt contracts, Dagster asset checks, Pandera, Great Expectations) compared qualitatively

standards.peer_review: accepted at CDMS workshop @ VLDB 2026 (workshop, short)
standards.artifacts: repo github.com/BauplanLabs/long_abstracts_and_other_stories listed; SDK client side said to be open source, SDK 2.0 in beta; server-side enforcement is proprietary

biases.detail: 'Millions of jobs' and recurring failure claims are operator assertions with no reported statistics.
Only hand-built Titanic failure scenarios, each designed to be caught by the new annotations.
Schema contracts on DAG nodes overlap heavily with dbt model contracts, Pandera, Pydantic; novelty is cross-language + catalog-aware composition, not measured.
No quantitative evaluation of any claim.

coi.affiliations: Bauplan Labs (all four authors; corresponding author is PI)
coi.detail: Product design announcement by the vendor presenting its own SDK favorably, with no independent or even internal quantitative check.

verdict_reason: Vendor design write-up with zero quantitative evidence; useful as a pattern description (typed contracts at pipeline boundaries, fail-fast at three stages) but cannot count as evidence in the KB.
applicability: The idea transfers conceptually, not as evidence: for a Java team whose cross-repository work spans several repositories, declaring the payload schema at each repo boundary (e.g., shared JSON Schema/Avro/OpenAPI or Java record types in a contracts module) and checking it at build time, in CI against the consumer's expectations, and at runtime before persisting or delivering to callers is the same 'shift-left contract' pattern, and fits spec-driven development. The Python/Arrow/Iceberg implementation and Bauplan-specific MCP flow do not transfer; there is no data on whether contracts reduce agent errors, so the team would need its own measurement.
